abstract: Rye has been an important food crop and source of nutrition in Finland for centuries and remains so today. Rye landraces and old varieties are still grown on farmers' fields. Interest in local landraces and conservation varieties has grown during the last decade due to climate change and its negative effects on biodiversity and resilience. We explored genetic diversity and population structure in Nordic rye landraces, historic population varieties and reference materials using complementary SSR and SNP datasets. For comparative analysis of genetic diversity, the Finnish varieties 'Riihi' and 'Reetta', the German inbred line Lo7, a German hybrid variety, the Estonian variety 'Elvi', and the landrace 'Sangaste' were included as reference materials. Both SSR and SNP analyses revealed geographically associated genetic differentiation within an otherwise largely shared Nordic rye gene pool. Notably, the independently sampled Mustialan and NordGen accessions of the Norwegian 'Tvengsberg' landrace were each clearly differentiated from the remaining rye material in the SSR and SNP datasets, respectively. Finnish landraces ('Aunus', 'Hermanni', 'Iivo', 'Joppe', 'Paakkola', and 'Taavetti') showed broadly similar genetic profiles, although substantial admixture was evident. In the SSR analysis, the Estonian accessions 'Sangaste' and 'Elvi' clustered together with 'Reetta', 'Riihi', and the Finnish landrace 'Polvijarvi', suggesting a closer genetic relationship among these accessions, although 'Polvijarvi' has previously been considered a distinct Finnish landrace. The Finnish variety 'Hankkijan Jussi' formed a separate cluster; this variety originates from a selection derived from the 60Co-irradiated Russian variety 'Vjatka'. The modern inbred line Lo7 and an unnamed hybrid variety were included as outgroup controls and showed clear genetic divergence from the Fennoscandian landrace material. Although Nordic rye landraces are often assumed to share a common ancestry and may have been influenced by historical seed exchange among farming communities, both SSR and SNP analyses revealed geographically associated genetic differentiation. These results indicate that regional genetic differentiation has been maintained despite the outcrossing nature of rye and the potential for historical gene flow.
